newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Ex-PM Keating says Australia in racial harmony.
newsitem.headline: Ex-PM Keating says Australia in racial harmony.

text.p: Former Australian Prime Minister Paul Keating said on Thursday that racial harmony rather than discord characterised Australia, despite a raging debate on racism and immigration.

Keating told a business conference in Jakarta that during his nearly 30 years of representing a multi-ethnic working class constituency, which included more than 10,000 Vietnamese, in Sydney's suburbs, he had never seen any incidents of racism.
"Not once did I ever see one nasty manifestation of residual resentment toward other people," Keating said in response to a question on the issue.
"That's the real picture and not some debate that is thrown up by somebody who drifts into the political system with views irrelevant to the modern world and rooted in ignorance," he said.
Australia's government and opposition united on Wednesday to condemn racial prejudice as a painful national debate on racism and immigration rumbled on.
Prime Minister John Howard accepted an opposition proposal for a joint parliamentary motion condemning racism and pledging tolerance.
Asian newspapers have criticised Howard for failing to take a tough stand against independent politician Pauline Hanson, who sparked the race debate.
Hanson complained in her maiden parliamentary speech last month that Australia was being swamped by Asians and called for an immediate halt to immigration.
Keating said that until 1947 Australia had been a mono-culture with a population of mostly English, Irish and Scottish descent.
"There are still people in that country who would like that to remain so and when things are said about it, they will respond to it," he said.
But he said serious evolutionary changes had taken place since that time and large numbers of Australians were either born overseas or were the children of migrants.

Keating was prime minister of Australia from 1991 until his defeat in elections in March this year. He was appointed a professor at the University of New South Wales, specialising in Australian-Asian relations, in May.
